title: Boss: The finished report
summary: Lay out the final report, split the program into three classes without changing a character of output, then add budgets.

steps.title: Ship it
body: Every part of the tool works. What is left is what turns working code into something you would hand to a colleague: a report laid out for a person to read, code organised so the next change is easy, and one new feature to prove it.
Three steps, no new syntax. Each one starts from your own code.
1. **The final layout.** A proper report: a title, the period covered, tables with headings and counts, and the grand total at the bottom.
2. **Refactor.** Split the program into three classes with one job each. The output must not change by a single character.
3. **Budgets.** An optional first line sets a budget per category, and the report says who is over.

steps.title: The final layout
prompt: Rearrange the output into the final report. The numbers are ones you already compute. For the example input from stage 4, print exactly:
- The title `EXPENSE REPORT`, then `Period:` with the earliest and the latest expense date.

- Two tables, **Category** (largest total first) and **Month** (oldest first). Each starts with an empty line, a heading row and a rule of 32 dashes. `SummaryRow` gains a count: `SummaryRow(string Name, int Count, decimal Total)`. A row is the name left-aligned in 12, the count right-aligned in 6, the total right-aligned in 14 as `N2`. The heading row uses the same widths with the words `Count` and `Total`.
- Two lists, `Needs review (N)` and `Rejected rows (N)`. Each starts with an empty line and has its items indented by two spaces. An empty list prints `  none`.
- The totals: an empty line, a rule of 32 `=`, a `Total` row laid out like a table row, then `Average` and `Largest` with the label left-aligned in 18 and the amount right-aligned in 14.
The old summary section is gone: its numbers moved to the bottom. `Largest` is now only the amount.
If there are no valid expenses, print the title, `No valid expenses.`, and the rejected rows, and nothing else:
The two tables share one method and the two lists share another. Keep the width 32 in a named constant.

steps.title: Three classes, three jobs
prompt: The program works, but it is one long file of loose methods. Parsing, policy and printing are three different jobs, and they change for three different reasons: a new input format, a new company rule, a new layout. Give each its own class.
| `ExpenseParser` | turning a line into a `ParseResult` | `ParseLine(int lineNumber, string line)` |
| `PolicyChecker` | the limits and the rules | `Check(Expense expense)` returning `List<Flag>`, and `Explain(Flag flag)` |
| `ReportWriter` | every `Console.WriteLine` of the report | `Write(List<Expense> expenses, List<Rejected> rejected)` |
Make them `static` classes: none of them has any state to remember. Members that only the class itself uses should not be `public`. Constants move into the class that uses them.
What remains at the top of the file is the whole program at a glance: read the lines, hand each to `ExpenseParser.ParseLine`, then call `ReportWriter.Write`.
This is a **refactor**: the structure changes and the behaviour does not. The tests are the same as in the last step, and the output must be identical.
> **Tip:** Move one class at a time and run the tests after each. Classes go at the bottom of the file with the other types.

Inside a static class every method needs `static`. Give `public` only to the members in the table. `MealLimit` and `LargeExpenseLimit` become `const` fields of `PolicyChecker`, and the width becomes a `const` field of `ReportWriter`.

`ReportWriter.Write` contains what the top of the file did after the loop. Its helpers call `PolicyChecker.Check(e)` and `PolicyChecker.Explain`. The top of the file ends with `ReportWriter.Write(expenses, rejected);`.

steps.title: Budgets
prompt: A new requirement arrives: finance wants to know which categories are over budget. With the code in three classes, you know where each part of the change goes.
**Input.** A line that starts with `#budget` sets budgets. It is normally the first line:

After `#budget` come entries separated by commas, each of the form `Category=Limit`. Spaces around entries, names and limits are ignored, and category names follow the same rules as in an expense row. An entry is invalid if it does not have exactly one `=`, the category is unknown, or the limit is not a positive number. An invalid entry becomes a rejected row with the reason `invalid budget 'ENTRY'`. The other entries on the line still count.
**Output.** If there is at least one budget, a new table goes between the Category and Month tables:
- The heading row is `Budget` left-aligned in 12, then `Limit` and `Actual` each right-aligned in 10, followed by the rule of 32 dashes.
- One row per budget, in the order they were given: the category in 12, the limit and the actual spending each in 10 as `N2`, two spaces, then the status.
- The status is `over by X`, `under by X` or `on budget`, where `X` is the difference as `N2`. A category with a budget and no expenses has an actual of `0.00`.
With no budgets the report is exactly as before. With no valid expenses the budget table is not printed.

**Where it goes.** Add the record `Budget(Category Category, decimal Limit)` and a third result, `ParsedBudget(Budget Budget) : ParseResult`. `ExpenseParser` gains `ParseBudgetLine(int lineNumber, string line)` returning a `List<ParseResult>`, one per entry. `ReportWriter.Write` takes the budgets as well: `Write(expenses, budgets, rejected)`.

tests.name: budgets under, over and exactly met
no budget line: the report is unchanged
a budget with no spending, and untidy spacing
invalid budgets and no valid expenses

hints: Parser first. `line.Substring("#budget".Length)` is everything after the marker. Split it on `,` with `StringSplitOptions.TrimEntries | StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries`, then split each entry on `=`.

An entry is good when it has 2 parts, the first is a category (pull your category check out into a `TryParseCategory` method so both parsers share it), and the second passes `decimal.TryParse` and is over 0. Return `new ParsedBudget(new Budget(category, limit))`, otherwise a `Rejected`.

In the report, the actual spending is `expenses.Where(e => e.Category == budget.Category).Sum(e => e.Amount)`. The status is a `switch` on `actual - limit`: `> 0 => $"over by {difference:N2}"`, `< 0 => $"under by {-difference:N2}"`, `_ => "on budget"`. A row is `$"{budget.Category,-12}{budget.Limit,10:N2}{actual,10:N2}  {status}"`.

steps.title: What you built
body: That is a complete, honest command-line tool. Along the way you used most of what makes everyday C# pleasant:
- **Reading input** until `ReadLine` returns `null`, and keeping line numbers so errors point somewhere.
- **A domain model**: a record and enums in place of loose strings, `DateOnly` for dates, and `decimal` for money.
- **Results in place of exceptions**: `TryParse` guard clauses and a `ParseResult` that is either `Parsed` or `Rejected`, so one bad row never costs the whole report.
- **LINQ** to count, sum, average, group and order.
- **Composite formatting**: `N2`, and widths that make columns line up.
- **Pattern matching** to write policy rules that read like the policy.
- **Small classes with one job each**, which is why the budget feature had an obvious home.

The shape you ended with, *parse, then check, then report*, is the shape of a great many real programs. Importers, log analysers, billing runs and data clean-up scripts are all this tool with different nouns.
> **Tip:** Good next steps on your own: read from a file named on the command line, add a `--csv` output mode with a second writer class, or load the policy limits from the input the way budgets are.
